prize_parts.citation: for the development of aberration correction in electron optics, which brought routine sub-angstrom imaging and spectroscopy of atoms in matter

statement.case_for: Aberration correction is a discovery-or-invention in the sense the prize statutes intend: a long-standing, theoretically proven limit of round electron lenses (Scherzer's theorem) was overcome by multipole correctors designed by Rose and built by Haider and colleagues, and Urban's group demonstrated that corrected instruments deliver atomic-resolution information on real materials. The outcome is measurable and unambiguous, the resolution gain is roughly an order of magnitude, and it has been independently reproduced in thousands of laboratories. It changed what experimental physics can observe: oxygen and other light atoms, individual defects and interfaces, and in situ dynamics, which in turn feed condensed-matter theory and materials physics. The three credited names are a coherent set (theory and optical design, corrector construction, application to materials). Reading the opening ballots, this is also the candidate whose maturity is least in doubt: four decades of development, no dispute about whether the effect is real, and no pending interpretive question as with the pairing mechanism in twisted graphene or the source population in neutrino astronomy.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is category and attribution. Colleagues have said this may read as methodology or engineering rather than physics, with a boundary toward chemistry and materials science, and I take that seriously even though the physics of electron optics is central. Attribution is also not fully clean: the STEM-corrector strand (Krivanek and Dellby, and Zach) is not covered by the three credited names, so a Rose-Haider-Urban prize risks being read as crediting only the TEM strand. Finally, it is only ranked by three of eight members, so it lacks the breadth of support that the optical lattice clock or topological insulator candidates have, and I should not mistake my own first place for committee-wide merit.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B052 fourth as a genuine instrumentation breakthrough with a coherent trio, but worries that Krivanek and the STEM-corrector line have an equally strong claim and that the work may be seen as chemistry or materials science rather than physics.
responses.response: I agree the Krivanek-Dellby STEM-corrector strand is a real attribution problem and I do not wave it away; it is why I rate the allocation as not fully clean. I still think the Rose-Haider-Urban trio is the defensible core, since the theoretical corrector design, its first working realisation and its first demonstration of atomic-resolution gain in materials are the origin of the field, while the STEM line followed a few years later. On the physics-versus-chemistry boundary I disagree: the object is electron optics and the measured quantity is resolution of matter at the atomic scale, which is the same kind of recognised achievement as the 1986 microscopy prize. I also note Pearce's own hesitation about B009 for collaboration-scale credit, and by that yardstick B052 has a bounded group of originators, which is an advantage.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B052 seventh, recognising its value to materials theorists but asking whether it is a physics discovery or engineering, and noting that Krivanek and Zach are not credited.
responses.response: The question is fair and I would not answer it by pointing to usefulness alone. The prize is for a discovery or invention, as I understand the criterion and as I said in my lecture earlier this year (as reported by Tohoku University, not an official transcript), and an invention that removes a fundamental limit and enables new observations qualifies if the consequences are in physics. Here they are: direct imaging of interfaces, vacancies and defects in oxides and two-dimensional materials supplies the structural input for the electronic-structure calculations Eriksson himself relies on. Where I concede ground is that I cannot show that B052 is more transformative than the correlated-electron candidates, and I would not insist on it against a broad majority.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock B053 first: the magic-wavelength proposal by Katori and Ye's record accuracy are cleanly separable from earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes, the independent confirmation is strong, and redefinition of the second is approaching.
responses.response: I largely agree and rank B053 third; of all the candidates it has the cleanest two-person attribution and the broadest support across the table. My reservation is modest: Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) cover enabling tools and a neighbouring clock family, so the citation would need to say what is new, namely lattice trapping at the magic wavelength and the resulting 1e-18 accuracy. I do not think that overlap is disqualifying. Where I differ from Kroll is only on ordering, and I would accept B053 as a prize if the committee preferred it, so I name it as my first alternative rather than as a competitor to be defeated.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery B046 first as the natural complement to the 2013 theory prize, with exceptional maturity but a real difficulty in selecting three people from two collaborations.
responses.response: The scientific case is very strong and I do not dispute it; the Higgs observation is arguably the most consequential experimental result of the period. My concern is the one Danielsson himself raises. Choosing three from Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra for a result achieved by thousands is arbitrary in a way that would be hard to defend in the citation, and the four-name credited list already signals that the committee would be rewarding roles rather than a bounded discovery. That is why I would not place B046 in my preferred configuration even though its importance exceeds that of my own first choice; a prize this size needs a configuration the committee can justify person by person.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards aberration-corrected electron microscopy as physics rather than methodology is a judgement I cannot settle from the opening ballots.
Whether the STEM-corrector strand (Krivanek, Dellby, Zach) should displace or join a credited name, which the three-person limit makes impossible to resolve fairly.
Whether, without wide support, a three-laureate instrumentation prize can compete against candidates ranked by most members, notably B053 and B013.
statement.conflict_note: I am an experimental electron microscopist, and my own research group uses aberration-corrected and in situ transmission electron microscopy, so I have a field and user connection to B052 even though the provided profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Rose, Haider or Urban. This may warrant recusal from the decision on B052, or at least that my first-place ranking be weighed with that proximity in mind. My Chalmers affiliation overlaps with Goran Johansson, who ranked B001 first, and I see no direct conflict for the other shortlisted candidates.
